opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Right now Canvas is very synchronous: you're sitting there, you ask the model to edit some code, it rewrites a section, you review it, and you go back and forth. That's useful, but it's still a pair-programming loop where the human is the bottleneck on every turn.

What gets me excited is moving from that turn-by-turn interaction to something closer to how you'd work with a really good colleague. You hand off a task like "refactor this module," "add tests for these edge cases," or "figure out why this build is flaky," and the model goes off and does it on its own time. With computer use, it doesn't have to live inside the text box. It can open a terminal, run the code, look at the browser output, read the docs, and iterate until something actually works. Then it comes back to you with a result, not just a suggestion.

Canvas becomes the place where that work gets surfaced and reviewed. Instead of a chat log, you'd see something like a diff, plus the trace of what the agent tried, what failed, and why it chose a particular approach. You stay in control of the important decisions, but you're not babysitting every keystroke.

There are a few hard problems in getting there. One is trust and verification. If the model has been working for twenty minutes autonomously, how do you quickly tell whether it did the right thing? That's partly a UX question, about showing the right level of detail, and partly a model-behavior question, about the model knowing when to stop and ask instead of plowing ahead on a bad assumption. Another is interruptibility. You want to be able to jump in mid-task, redirect it, or leave a comment on a specific line, and have the agent incorporate that without starting over.

I also think of it as multiplayer in a sense. You might have several agents working on different branches of a problem in parallel, and the human acts more like a manager or editor, merging the good ideas and giving feedback. Canvas is a natural surface for that because it's already about co-creating an artifact rather than just exchanging messages.

So the long-term vision is that the model becomes a real collaborator that can take initiative, use the same tools you do, and work asynchronously, while the interface keeps humans in the loop at the moments that matter. We're early, but that's the direction I find most compelling.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent autonomously running code and iterating on delegated tasks, but does not say it tests a coding feature in its own virtual environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that Canvas was always meant to be a shared workspace, not just a text box that happens to render code. Right now the interaction is still very synchronous. You ask for something, you watch it type, you react. And that's fine for small edits, but it's not how people actually collaborate on real work. When I work with a colleague, I don't stand over their shoulder. I leave a comment, I go do something else, and I come back to a diff or a note that says "here's what I did, here's what I wasn't sure about."

So the vision is that Canvas becomes the surface where you hand off work to an agent that has an actual computer. You might say, "take this prototype, get it running against the staging API, and tell me where it breaks." Then you close the laptop. The agent goes off, spins up an environment, runs things, maybe clicks through a UI to reproduce a bug, and when you come back there's a trail in the Canvas: the changes it made, screenshots of what it saw, a short list of decisions it had to make without you. That last part is really important to me. The agent should surface its uncertainty rather than hiding it behind a confident final answer.

The hard design problem is attention. If the agent can work for an hour, you don't want an hour of logs. You want something closer to a pull request from a thoughtful teammate: a summary at the top, the ability to expand into detail where you care, and inline places where you can push back. I think comments are actually the right primitive here. You should be able to highlight a block in Canvas, leave a note like "this feels fragile," and have that become a task the agent picks up later, asynchronously, without you re-explaining the whole context.

And then there's trust. Computer use raises the stakes because the agent isn't just writing text, it's taking actions in a real environment. So a lot of the work is about making the agent's intentions legible before it acts, and making it easy to scope what it's allowed to touch. I'd rather have an agent that pauses and says "I'm about to change the database schema, is that okay?" than one that's fast and surprising. The goal is that you feel like you're collaborating with something that respects your time and your boundaries, which honestly is the same thing we want from human collaborators.

r001.rationale: The response describes handing a prototype task to an agent, which spins up an environment and runs it against a staging API to find where it breaks.

astra-6.text:
I imagine Canvas becoming a shared workspace where you can delegate a piece of work to an agent and then come back to review it. You might say, “Can you build this feature and test it in the browser?” And the agent can work asynchronously—write the code, interact with the interface, and check whether the result actually works.

The interesting design question is how you stay in control without having to watch every step. I’d want the agent to leave enough context for me to understand what it changed, what it checked, and where it needs my judgment. Then I can give feedback directly on the artifact, and it can continue. That makes the collaboration feel less like a sequence of chat messages and more like an ongoing project.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent can build the feature and test it in a browser, but does not communicate that it tests the feature in its own virtual environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I imagine it feeling less like a chat where you have to wait for every response and more like working with a teammate in a shared workspace. In Canvas, you could hand an agent a task, continue working on another part of the code, and come back to review its changes.

The interesting part with computer use is that the agent could also run the application, interact with it, and check whether the behavior matches what you asked for. It could bring back a proposed change and show you what it tested, or flag a decision where it needs your input.

For that to work well asynchronously, you need visibility into what the agent is doing and a clear way to review, edit, or undo its work. I’d want Canvas to make that handoff feel natural, so you can delegate without having to supervise every step.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent could run and interact with the application to check its behavior, but does not say it tests the feature in its own virtual environment.
